source.title: Benign overfitting in linear regression
source.authors: P. Bartlett; Philip M. Long; G. Lugosi; Alexander Tsigler

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some mathematical notation is flattened or garbled in places, but the text is readable and the main results are stated.
record.tranche_reason: The paper gives theoretical results about when minimum-norm interpolating linear regression predicts accurately. It does not test a double-descent curve over model size, epochs, or sample size, nor does it test the other listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites earlier deep-network interpolation results as motivation, but reports no new deep-network experiment or double-descent sweep. Its own results characterize the prediction risk of interpolating linear regression; those findings are recorded under fits_no_version because they do not establish the curve shape required by any listed version.
record.test_reason: This is a theory paper. It characterizes when the minimum-norm interpolating linear regressor has near-optimal excess risk (benign overfitting), using two effective ranks of the covariance. It never sweeps capacity, epochs or samples to trace a risk curve. Its results say whether the interpolator is benign in a given regime. They do not show risk falling, peaking and falling again. So it bears on interpolation risk, not on the double-descent shape any version names.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors characterize when min-norm interpolation in linear regression is benign, in terms of two effective ranks. They find that overparameterization (many unimportant low-variance directions) is essential. Large but finite dimension allows benign overfitting for a much wider range of covariances than infinite dimension. They leave extension to neural networks open.
record.recipe_differences: The paper provides a finite-sample theoretical risk characterization for minimum-norm interpolating linear regression rather than conducting model-size, epoch, or sample-size double-descent sweeps.

fits_no_version.finding: The minimum-norm interpolator in linear regression is near-optimal iff k*/n, n/R_k*(Σ) and r0(Σ)/n are small. Its expected excess risk is at least σ²/c when k* ≥ n/c1. In finite dimension, being benign requires p_n = ω(n) plus a small but not exponentially small isotropic component.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign overfitting in min-norm linear regression requires many low-variance directions, far more than the sample size, as measured by covariance effective ranks.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
record.problems: The paper's own results concern linear regression and depend on stated distributional assumptions; the authors say those assumptions do not apply directly to the neural-tangent-kernel setting and leave extension to neural networks open. It reports no direct deep-network test-error curves for the claim.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant results omitted. Cited empirical deep-network findings are not the paper's own results and are not recorded as rows.

untested.parts: No deep-network model-size sweep; the paper's results are for linear regression only.
No sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold.

No risk-versus-capacity curve. The text does say the excess risk is at least a constant at p=n with identity covariance, and that benign overfitting needs dimension p_n = ω(n) (Theorem 31(3,4)). These are statements about two regimes, not a curve, and the paper does not present them as double descent.
Effective ranks r_k and R_k characterize risk. Nothing tests whether one complexity measure predicts the peak location across size, epochs and samples.
No regularization analysis and no multiple-peak analysis. Label noise appears only as the σ² variance term in the risk bounds.
No re-indexing of a double-descent curve by effective parameter count.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly linked to none. Their 'observed' states refer to the theorems' own statements, not to any version. Two results come closest to V4: the p=n, Σ=I argument in Section 5 (excess risk bounded below by a constant) and the ω(n) dimension requirement. Both are regime statements without a capacity sweep. A reviewer might argue for T5 on V4, but the paper makes no double-descent argument. It cites Belkin et al. 1812.11118 only as related work.

versions.untested_parts: No test-error sweep over deep-network model size or peak near the training-set interpolation size.
No test-error measurement over training epochs.
No sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold measuring whether more data raises test error.
The paper studies interpolating linear predictors, but does not sweep model-class capacity or establish that risk falls again as capacity grows past interpolation.
The paper uses two effective-rank quantities to characterize interpolation risk, but does not test whether one measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and sample size.
No test of peak dependence on label noise or regularization, multiple descent peaks, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
No comparison of a double-descent curve with a curve indexed by an effective parameter count.

rows.subject: minimum norm estimator θ̂
rows.size_stated: Parameter-space dimension is large enough for exact fitting; the paper assumes more parameters than the sample size.
rows.operation_detail: Theoretically bounds excess prediction risk of the minimum-norm interpolating estimator.

conditions.value: k* < n/c1, where k* is the first index with r_k(Σ) ≥ bn
Risk bound depends on r0(Σ), k*, and R_k*(Σ)

rows.measure: Excess prediction risk R(θ̂) and its expectation
rows.baseline: Prediction risk of the optimal linear predictor θ*
rows.value: With probability at least 1 − δ, the paper gives an upper bound consisting of a θ* term and terms involving r0(Σ), k*, and R_k*(Σ); it also gives E R(θ̂) ≥ (σ²/c)(k*/n + n/R_k*(Σ)). The authors state that near-optimal prediction requires the relevant terms to be small.
rows.note: This is a theoretical characterization of when an interpolating linear estimator can predict well, not a measurement of risk changing with model capacity.
